## Summary Scores

-   **Sensitivity:** Low
-   **Exposure:** Moderate
-   **Vulnerability:** Low

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Define the directory and the correct file extension pattern
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), "\\.pdf$", "\\.png$")
dir_path <- here::here("figures/Spiny dogfish")

# Search for any file containing the string AND the correct extension
found_files <- list.files(
  path = dir_path, 
  pattern = paste0("combined_table_allvars.*", ext), 
  full.names = TRUE
)

has_figure <- length(found_files) > 0

if (has_figure) {
  # Get metadata for all matching files
  file_details <- file.info(found_files)
  
  # Find the row with the maximum (newest) modification time
  newest_index <- which.max(file_details$mtime)
  
  # Assign the newest file's path to img_path
  img_path <- found_files[newest_index]
} else {
  img_path <- NULL
}
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| lightbox: true
#| out-width: "100%"
#| label: fig-sum-tab-spinydog
#| fig-cap: "Summary Sensitivity, Exposure, and Vulnerability Scores and Score Distributions for Spiny dogfish. Exposure and Vulnerability scores are averaged spatially across the species distribution and within stocks if applicable (see @fig-vuln-spinydog and @fig-exp-spinydog). Life History Data Quality (LH DQ) and Standard Deviations (SD) are reported for senstivity and exposure/vulnerability scores, respectively."
#| fig-pos: "H"
#| fig-align: "center"
knitr::include_graphics(img_path)
```

## Score Descriptions:

### Sensitivity:

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Define the directory and the correct file extension pattern
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), "\\.pdf$", "\\.png$")
dir_path <- here::here("figures/Spiny dogfish")

# Search for any file containing the string AND the correct extension
found_files <- list.files(
  path = dir_path, 
  pattern = paste0("sensitivity.*", ext), 
  full.names = TRUE
)

has_figure <- length(found_files) > 0

if (has_figure) {
  # Get metadata for all matching files
  file_details <- file.info(found_files)
  
  # Find the row with the maximum (newest) modification time
  newest_index <- which.max(file_details$mtime)
  
  # Assign the newest file's path to img_path
  img_path <- found_files[newest_index]
} else {
  img_path <- NULL
}

# Store the TRUE/FALSE result 
has_figure <- file.exists(img_path)
```

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| lightbox: true
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| fig-cap: "Spiny dogfish Sensitivity on the Northeast Shelf"
#| label: fig-sens-spinydog
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-pos: "H"

knitr::include_graphics(img_path)
```

Spiny dogfish received a **Low** sensitivity score, with a certainty of 100%. The only attribute with a score greater than 2.5 was Population Growth Rate (3.6) (@fig-sum-tab-spinydog). They are a long-lived, slowly maturing species. Age at maturity ranges from 6 years for males and 12 years for females, with maximum lifespans of 35-40 years [@stehlik2007]. Gestation periods last from 18-24 months [@stehlik2007].

Spiny dogfish also received a Low sensitivity score in the previous Climate Vulnerability Assessment. This score was also driven by Population Growth Rates [@hare2016vulnerability].

Mean Exposure scores for Spiny dogfish were **Moderate** (2 +/- 0.94) (@fig-sum-tab-spinydog). Exposure was Very High over Georges Bank and High along the coast of the Gulf of Maine and in Southern New England. Scores were also High on the continental shelf break (@fig-exp-spinydog). These patterns were driven by bottom temperature, oxygen, salinity, and aragonite saturation scores (@fig-fact-exp-spinydog). 

In the previous Assessment, spiny dogfish received a High Exposure score, driven by high sea surface temperature and ocean acidification exposure scores [@hare2016vulnerability].

Mean Vulnerability scores for Spiny dogfish were Low (2 +/- 0.94) (@fig-sum-tab-spinydog). Exposure was mostly uniform across the model species range. There were some Moderate scores over Georges Bank (@fig-vuln-spinydog).

In the previous Assessment, spiny dogfish also received a Low Vulnerability score [@hare2016vulnerability].

## Data Quality Metrics

### Life History Data Quality:

90% of data quality scores were greater than or equal to 2, indicating excellent data quality. No data gaps (mean attribute data quality score \< 2) were identified (@fig-sum-tab-spinydog).

### Model Confidence Score:

The ensemble spiny dogfish model received a mean model confidence score of 0.9 (+/- 0.3), indicating no confidence in the model. The predicted distributions did not meet experts’ expectations. Experts suggested that the model may be overfit. The ensemble model AUC score was 0.77, indicating fair model performance.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
*Note: For an animated version of this plot, please see the online version of this document.*
:::

Spiny dogfish core habitat and range shrunk significantly between 1993 and 2023. Spiny dogfish lost core habitat off the coast of Virginia and the southern edge of their range moved northward during this time period (@fig-shifts-spinydog). The weighted centroid shifted 10 km north-northeast. 

Under near future ocean conditions, spiny dogfish core habitat and range are predicted to expand to near 1993 distributions, including reestablishing core habitat off the coast of Virginia (@fig-shifts-spinydog). The weighted centroid is predicted to shift 10 km back southwest. 

In the previous assessment, spiny dogfish received a Very High Distributional Vulnerability Rank due to their habitat preferences and high mobility [@hare2016vulnerability].

| 2031-2035 | 9.7 km SW | 115,098 (+4,287) | 262,657 (+3,383) | 7.05 (+0.19) | 9.14 (+0.08) |

### Directional Effect:

Experts predict that climate change will have a **neutral** effect on spiny dogfish. Certainty was 91%. Occurrence of spiny dogfish is correlated with warmer temperatures [@sagarese2014a]. They are highly migratory and will move north-south to follow waters within their preferred temperature range (6-13C) [@stehlik2007] [@carlson2014]. They may benefit from the loss of cod as they occupy similar feeding niches [@neuenhoff2019] [@ono2019]. The previous Assessment also predicted that climate change would have a neutral impact on spiny dogfish [@hare2016vulnerability].

## Climate Effects on Abundance and Distribution

@nye2009 observed a range expansion and southward shift in center of biomass in spiny dogfish, although changes in biomass over the study period may have influenced these shifts. Seasonal occurrence of spiny dogfish is highly correlated with depth and bottom temperature, with a higher probability of occurrence in warmer years versus colder years [@sagarese2014a]. Spiny dogfish shift their distribution seasonally; variation in environmental drivers may impact population and fishery dynamics as temperatures continue to increase. Climate-inducing seasonal distribution shifts influencing habitat availability for spiny dogfish may also lead to vulnerability of the inshore fishery in the fall [@sagarese2014b].

## Life History Synopsis

Atlantic spiny dogfish are a schooling, highly migratory shark species (HMS) inhabiting inshore and offshore waters from Labrador to Florida, although they are most abundant from Nova Scotia and Cape Hatteras. Spiny dogfish perform diel vertical migrations; most schools are found around 40-50 m depth, but can descend upwards of 500 m [@stehlik2007] [@carlson2014]. There are populations that occupy the continental shelves of Europe, Asia, and the northeast Pacific, but these populations do not mix [@stehlik2007]. Spiny dogfish perform north-south migrations and move between inshore-offshore waters in response to water temperature, migrating north in the spring and summer and south in the fall and winter to remain in waters between 6-13°C [@stehlik2007] [@carlson2014]. Age at maturity is 6 years for males and 12 years for females, with a lifespan of 35 years for males and 40 years for females. Spawning occurs offshore in the winter, with a gestation period of 18-24 months [@stehlik2007]. Proportions of mature females in catch are correlated with bottom temperatures, with more mature females caught at relatively higher bottom temperatures. However, how temperature impacts reproduction is still unclear [@sagarese2014b]. Spiny dogfish are opportunistic feeders, preying upon a variety of fishes (herring, mackerel, hakes, sand lance, menhaden), squid, ctenophores, polychaetes, crustaceans, bivalves. Diets can shift based on location and availability [@stehlik2007] [@devries2025]. Predators of spiny dogfish include sharks, seals, cod, goosefish, dolphins, and larger fish [@stehlik2007]. Spiny dogfish occupy a similar niche to that of Atlantic cod, whose populations have been impacted by increasing seal populations in the Northwest Atlantic and Canada. It has been hypothesized that the loss of cod could be a benefit to spiny dogfish, since they occupy similar feeding niches [@neuenhoff2019] [@ono2019]. The Mid-Atlantic Fishery Management Council (MAFMC) leads the joint management of the Spiny Dogfish Fishery Management Plan, with support from the New England Fishery Management Council (NEFMC) and Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission (ASMFC) [@mafmc2025_spinydog]. The ASMFC manages spiny dogfish in state waters via the Interstate Fishery Management Plan for Spiny Dogfish [@asmfc2002_spinydog]. As of 2023, spiny dogfish in the Northwest Atlantic are not overfished and overfishing is not occurring [@nefsc2023_spinydog].

#| label: fig-radar-spinydog

Bottom temperature, oxygen, and salinity, as well as large zooplankton biomass were important dynamic drivers of spiny dogfish distributions (@fig-radar-spinydog). Temperatures drive migration patterns [@stehlik2007] [@carlson2014]. Spiny dogfish are also generalist piscivores [@stehlik2007] [@devries2025]. When exposure was calculated using only these important factors, scores remained Moderate and distributions of scores remained relatively similar (@fig-sum-imp-spinydog; @fig-exp-imp-spinydog).
